title: "The Reproduction Number"
subtitle: "Module 1: Low-Dimensional Dynamics"

---

The basic reproduction number $R_0$ is the average number of secondary infections caused by one infectious individual in a fully susceptible population [@hethcote2000mathematics; @keeling2008modeling].

## R0 in the SIR model

In the SIR model of [Compartmental Models](compartmental-models.qmd), one infectious person infects susceptibles at rate $\beta S \approx \beta$ when $S \approx 1$, during an infectious period of mean length $1/\gamma$. Hence

$$
R_0 = \frac{\beta}{\gamma} .
$$ {#eq-r0}

## The threshold

The infectious equation is $\dot I = \gamma I (R_0 S - 1)$. At the start of an outbreak $S(0) \approx 1$, so

- $R_0 > 1$: $I$ grows at rate $\gamma(R_0 - 1) = \beta - \gamma$, and an epidemic occurs;
- $R_0 < 1$: $I$ decays and the infection dies out.

This is the threshold theorem of Kermack and McKendrick [@kermack1927contribution; @hethcote2000mathematics]. During the epidemic, the relevant quantity is the effective reproduction number $R_{\text{eff}}(t) = R_0 S(t)$. The number of infectious people peaks exactly when $R_{\text{eff}} = 1$, that is when $S = 1/R_0$.

The same threshold appears in the SIS model. The endemic equilibrium of $\dot I = \beta I(1 - I) - \gamma I$ is

$$
I^* = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0},
$$

which exists and is stable only for $R_0 > 1$ [@hethcote2000mathematics].

## Herd immunity

Suppose a fraction $p$ of the population is immune before the outbreak, so $S(0) = 1 - p$. An outbreak cannot start if $R_0 (1 - p) < 1$. The critical immunization fraction is

$$
p_c = 1 - \frac{1}{R_0} .
$$ {#eq-herd}

Vaccinating more than $p_c$ of the population protects the whole population, including those not vaccinated [@hethcote2000mathematics; @keeling2008modeling]. The formula assumes random mixing and a vaccine that gives full, lasting immunity.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-herd
#| fig-cap: "Critical immunization fraction p_c = 1 - 1/R0."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.5
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

r0 = np.linspace(1, 15, 300)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(r0, 1 - 1 / r0)
ax.set_xlabel("R0")
ax.set_ylabel("p_c")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## What R0 does not tell you

- $R_0$ depends on the disease and on the population: the same pathogen has different $R_0$ values in different contact patterns [@hethcote2000mathematics].
- In the SIR model, only $\beta$ and $\gamma$ together determine the shape of the outbreak. Early data, which grow like $e^{(\beta - \gamma)t}$, determine $\beta - \gamma$ but not $R_0$. You will see the consequences in [Predicting the Peak](peak-prediction.qmd).

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise
A disease has $\beta = 0.3$ per day and a mean infectious period of 10 days. Compute $R_0$, the early growth rate, the doubling time of cases, and the critical vaccination coverage.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$\gamma = 0.1$ per day, so $R_0 = 3$. The early growth rate is $\beta - \gamma = 0.2$ per day, giving a doubling time $\ln 2 / 0.2 \approx 3.5$ days. The critical coverage is $p_c = 1 - 1/3 \approx 0.67$.
:::
